title: Understanding inflammatory arthritis

General overview of arthritis

Arthritis encompasses a group of inflammatory joint diseases distinguished by persistent joint inflammation. Unlike osteoarthritis, a noninflammatory degenerative disease, arthritis manifests through intense pain, swelling, local warmth, and sometimes redness. It can affect one joint or several, and its course is often chronic, with painful flare-ups alternating with periods of relative remission.
Diversity of arthritis forms
Among the best-known forms are:

items: Rheumatoid arthritis: an autoimmune disease progressively destroying joints, causing deformities and disability.
Spondyloarthropathies: affecting the spine and sacroiliac joints, causing back pain, stiffness, and sometimes eye or skin involvement.
Infectious arthritis: caused by bacteria or viruses, requiring urgent management to avoid joint destruction.
Metabolic arthritis: such as gout, linked to accumulation of uric acid crystals in joints and causing extremely painful attacks.

blocks.text: These diseases cause substantial, sometimes disabling functional difficulty and can impair quality of life. They are not confined to local involvement: chronic inflammation can have general effects on the body, promoting fatigue, metabolic disorders, and diminished morale.

Conventional treatments rely on anti-inflammatory drugs, immunosuppressants, and biological therapies. They provide relief, sometimes striking, but do not cure the disease. The accumulation mechanism in arthritis

The accumulation theory offers a complementary explanation to conventional mechanisms of joint inflammation. According to Dr. Seignalet and other researchers, certain poorly digested dietary and bacterial molecules cross the intestinal barrier and enter the blood. Once circulating, they deposit in joints, disrupting local cell functioning and triggering an inappropriate immune reaction.
Stage 1 — A weakened intestinal barrier

When attacked by modern diets (mutated cereal grains, dairy products, harsh cooking methods, additives), the intestine becomes permeable. Tight junctions between intestinal cells open, allowing protein fragments, oxidized lipids, or bacterial toxins through. This phenomenon, called ‘intestinal hyperpermeability,’ is now recognized as a key factor in many inflammatory and autoimmune diseases.
Stage 2 — Passage into the blood

These foreign molecules, normally destroyed or neutralized, enter the bloodstream. The immune system identifies them as intruders. But instead of rapid elimination, they accumulate and attach to certain tissues, particularly joints, which become favored deposit sites.
Stage 3 — Deposition in joints

Joints, rich in connective tissue and synovial fluid, offer favorable conditions for these molecules to accumulate. They infiltrate cartilage and the synovial membrane, disrupting cellular balance. Local cells confronted by these deposits send distress signals activating the immune system.
Stage 4 — Immune reaction and inflammation
Immune cells, recognizing these deposits as foreign, attack joint tissues themselves. This autoimmune process causes:

items: Chronic inflammation with production of pro-inflammatory cytokines.
Persistent pain due to irritation of nerve endings.
Swelling and local warmth linked to increased blood flow and exudation.
Progressive cartilage and bone destruction, leading to joint deformity.

blocks.text: Why conventional treatments fail

Symptoms and disease course

Arthritis manifests through a set of characteristic clinical signs reflecting persistent joint inflammation. These symptoms, sometimes subtle initially, progressively become disabling and impair quality of life. Their course varies according to arthritis form, but all share a common point: they persist over time and require comprehensive management.
Typical symptoms

items: Intense joint pain: often nocturnal, waking patients and disturbing sleep. It worsens with prolonged rest and is partially relieved by movement.
Swelling and local warmth: the inflamed joint appears swollen, warm to touch, and sometimes red. This reflects increased blood flow and exudation linked to inflammation.
Prolonged morning stiffness: on waking, joints are stiff, sometimes requiring more than an hour to regain acceptable mobility.
General fatigue and fever: chronic inflammation acts as permanent stress on the body, causing fatigue, weight loss, and sometimes febrile episodes.
Long-term joint deformities: without appropriate management, cartilage and bone are destroyed, causing irreversible deformities and functional disability.

blocks.text: The course of arthritis
Each form of arthritis has its own pace of progression:

items: Rheumatoid arthritis often progresses through flare-ups, alternating inflammatory phases with partial remissions. Without treatment, it causes rapid joint destruction.
Spondyloarthropathies progress more slowly but cause increasing spinal stiffness, potentially reaching ankylosis.
Gout manifests through extremely painful acute attacks separated by periods of respite. Over time, uric acid deposits deform joints.
Infectious arthritis requires rapid intervention: its course can be fulminant and destroy a joint within days.
